singlet Z3 metal: χb​f\chi_{b}f 1 3×3=93\times 3=9 1
Type II triplet Z3 metal: d​Ψbd\,\Psi_{b} 1 3 3
SU(3) holon metal: ∑aχa​ψa​b\sum_{a}\chi_{a}\psi_{ab} 3 3×3=93\times 3=9 3×3=93\times 3=9

The singlet Z3 metal can keep its χb\chi_{b} fermions in the LLL, but its flavor-singlet holon ff must occupy nine distinct momenta. Type II triplet Z3 metal requires the flavor-singlet parton dd to fill three LLs, each containing three orbitals. Each of its three holon flavors must also occupy three distinct momenta. Neither product construction can therefore accommodate nine particles using only the LLL and 𝐤=0\mathbf{k}=0. The color construction supplies the missing internal states in both sectors without violating Pauli exclusion.

This counting gives a simple kinetic-energy motivation for the color ansatz. For the same parabolic parton dispersions, it avoids both the higher-LL cost of the Type II triplet Z3 metal and the nonzero-momentum cost of the two product states in this example. In the thermodynamic limit the holons form Fermi seas, but their nine pockets have density n/9n/9 each, compared with nn in the singlet Z3 metal and n/3n/3 in the Type II triplet Z3 metal. The resulting smaller Fermi momenta reduce the mean-field Fermi energy and kFk_{F}. Since our Hamiltonian contains only the kinetic energy, this color construction naturally saves energy compared with the two Z3 metals, whose holon wavefunctions necessarily involve a larger kFk_{F}.

S4.6 CB crystals: Hall crystals and skyrmions

A composite-boson condensate in statistical flux.

For the SU(3) anyon gas at α=1/3\alpha=1/3, we introduce a composite-boson field ϕ=(ϕ1,ϕ2,ϕ3)T\bm{\phi}=(\phi_{1},\phi_{2},\phi_{3})^{T}. Its components describe three internal states, as in a spinor Bose condensate [96, 97]. All three flavors couple to the same statistical gauge field aa. Including the electromagnetic probe AcA_{c}, the theory is Eq. (S51) with m=3m=3:

ℒ=ℒϕ​[a]+34​π​a​d​a+12​π​Ac​d​a.\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\phi}[a]+\frac{3}{4\pi}a\,da+\frac{1}{2\pi}A_{c}\,da. (S78)

With the probe turned off, flux attachment gives ba=−2πρ/3b_{a}=-2\pi\rho/3, where ρ=∑b|ϕb|2\rho=\sum_{b}|\phi_{b}|^{2}. At mean density nn, the three CB flavors together have signed filling ν∗=2​π​n/b¯a=−3\nu^{*}=2\pi n/\bar{b}_{a}=-3, or −1-1 per flavor for equal populations. The crystal ansatz accommodates this flux through a vortex lattice, with one vortex per statistical flux quantum in each flavor. Each component therefore has vortex density n/3n/3, with circulation of the same sign as bab_{a}. The three vortex sublattices can interleave, allowing the other flavors to fill each vortex core [98]. The total density can then remain nearly uniform while the flavor orientation varies periodically. This smooth orientation is the skyrmion texture of the crystal.

The CP2 texture and its skyrmions.

Where the total CB density is nonzero, the local flavor orientation is specified by

𝐙=ϕϕ†​ϕ,𝐙†​𝐙=1,𝐙∼ei​χ​𝐙.\mathbf{Z}=\frac{\bm{\phi}}{\sqrt{\bm{\phi}^{\dagger}\bm{\phi}}},\qquad\mathbf{Z}^{\dagger}\mathbf{Z}=1,\qquad\mathbf{Z}\sim e^{\mathrm{i}\chi}\mathbf{Z}. (S79)

Removing the common phase leaves two independent flavor weights and two relative phases. The resulting space is the complex projective plane, CP2, which has four real dimensions. Equivalently, its points are nonzero complex triples [ϕ1:ϕ2:ϕ3][\phi_{1}:\phi_{2}:\phi_{3}] identified under multiplication by any common nonzero complex number. A vortex in one component does not make this orientation singular if another component remains nonzero.

A texture on the sphere defines a map S2→CP2S^{2}\to\mathrm{CP}^{2}. The same description applies on the plane when the orientation is fixed at infinity. Such maps have an integer skyrmion number because π2​(CP2)=ℤ\pi_{2}(\mathrm{CP}^{2})=\mathbb{Z}. It is obtained from the Berry connection of the normalized spinor:

𝒜=−i​𝐙†​𝑑𝐙,Qsk=12​π​∫𝑑𝒜∈ℤ.\mathcal{A}=-\mathrm{i}\,\mathbf{Z}^{\dagger}d\mathbf{Z},\qquad Q_{\rm sk}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int d\mathcal{A}\in\mathbb{Z}. (S80)

Here d​𝒜d\mathcal{A} is the Berry curvature through the real-space surface.

One skyrmion from three vortices.

The two-component case provides useful intuition. A normalized spinor (Z1,Z2)T(Z_{1},Z_{2})^{T} defines a unit pseudospin 𝐧=𝐙†​𝝈​𝐙\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{Z}^{\dagger}\bm{\sigma}\mathbf{Z}, so that CP1 is the ordinary spin sphere. At a vortex of component 1, component 2 fills the core and nz=−1n_{z}=-1. If the components have equal weights away from the core, the spin approaches the equator, and the relative-phase winding rotates it around that equator. The texture covers one hemisphere and is a half-skyrmion, or meron. A vortex of component 2 has nz=+1n_{z}=+1 at its core and covers the other hemisphere. When the two vortices have the same circulation, their relative-phase windings are opposite and their skyrmion charges have the same sign. Together they form a unit skyrmion [99].

For three components, write Zb=pb​ei​θbZ_{b}=\sqrt{p_{b}}\,e^{\mathrm{i}\theta_{b}}, so that 𝒜=∑bpb​d​θb\mathcal{A}=\sum_{b}p_{b}\,d\theta_{b}. On a loop with constant flavor weights, a 2​π2\pi winding in just one component gives Berry flux 2​π​pb2\pi p_{b}. For equal weights this is half a flux quantum in SU(2), and one third in SU(3). Three separated component vortices, one of each flavor, can therefore carry one unit of skyrmion number together [100]. In our reference crystal at qb​g=−1/3q_{bg}=-1/3, each flavor has Nv=N/3N_{v}=N/3 vortices. The three lowest-LL orbitals have the same antiholomorphic degree NvN_{v} and no common zero, giving Qsk=−Nv=−N/3Q_{\rm sk}=-N_{v}=-N/3 in our convention. There are consequently 3​Nv3N_{v} component vortices but only NvN_{v} units of skyrmion number.

Classical energy of the interlaced crystal.

To estimate the energy of this texture, consider a periodic patch of the plane with mean density nn, CB mass MM and an SU(3)-invariant contact coupling g≥0g\geq 0. The ideal anyon gas has no contact interaction, but its classical average-field description acquires one: replacing the point fluxes by a smooth statistical field drops their short-distance self-interaction, and the resulting Chern–Simons–Schrödinger functional for bosons with attached flux contains an effective contact term whose strength depends on the flux profile and the intrinsic spin-orbit coupling of the anyons [101]. We therefore keep gg as a parameter of the classical estimate. We use the classical kinetic energy ℏ2​∫∑b|𝚷​ϕb|2/(2​M)\hbar^{2}\int\sum_{b}|\bm{\Pi}\phi_{b}|^{2}/(2M) and contact energy (g/2)​∫ρ2(g/2)\int\rho^{2}, where 𝚷=−i∇−𝐚\bm{\Pi}=-\mathrm{i}\nabla-\mathbf{a} and ba=−2πρ/3b_{a}=-2\pi\rho/3 locally. Since [Πx,Πy]=i​ba[\Pi_{x},\Pi_{y}]=\mathrm{i}b_{a}, integration by parts gives

Ecl=ℏ22​M​∫d2​r​∑b|(Πx−i​Πy)​ϕb|2+(π​ℏ23​M+g2)​∫d2​r​ρ2.E_{\rm cl}=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2M}\int d^{2}r\sum_{b}|(\Pi_{x}-\mathrm{i}\Pi_{y})\phi_{b}|^{2}+\left(\frac{\pi\hbar^{2}}{3M}+\frac{g}{2}\right)\int d^{2}r\,\rho^{2}.

The first term is nonnegative and ∫ρ2≥N​n\int\rho^{2}\geq Nn. Every classical condensate therefore satisfies Ecl/N≥elbE_{\rm cl}/N\geq e_{\rm lb}, with elb=π​ℏ2​n/(3​M)+g​n/2e_{\rm lb}=\pi\hbar^{2}n/(3M)+gn/2. Approaching this bound requires orbitals close to the lowest Landau level and a nearly uniform total density. Interlacing the vortices allows each component to vanish at its own cores while the other two fill them.

For an explicit trial field, take three equal-weight triangular LLL vortex lattices in the mean field b¯a=−B\bar{b}_{a}=-B, with B=2​π​n/3B=2\pi n/3. Each component has one vortex per cell of area 2​π/B2\pi/B. With primitive vectors 𝐚1,𝐚2\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2} at 60∘60^{\circ}, displace the three copies by 0,𝐝,2​𝐝0,\mathbf{d},2\mathbf{d}, where 𝐝=(𝐚1+𝐚2)/3\mathbf{d}=(\mathbf{a}_{1}+\mathbf{a}_{2})/3. Together the 3​Nv3N_{v} vortices then form a triangular lattice with spacing |𝐚1|/3|\mathbf{a}_{1}|/\sqrt{3}, whose three sublattices carry the three flavors (Fig. S5). Each vortex has six nearest neighbors, alternating between the other two flavors. This is not a kagome arrangement, which would require displacements by half lattice vectors.

For a reciprocal vector 𝐆\mathbf{G} with integer indices (h,k)(h,k), the LLL density Fourier coefficient has magnitude exp[−G2/(4B)]\exp[-G^{2}/(4B)] relative to its mean [98]. Averaging the displaced copies cancels every coefficient with h+k≢0(mod3)h+k\not\equiv 0\pmod{3}, including the six shortest reciprocal vectors. For f=ρ/nf=\rho/n this gives ⟨f2⟩=1.00011267\langle f^{2}\rangle=1.00011267, where the brackets denote a spatial average. The sum of the magnitudes of the nonzero harmonics is less than 0.027, so f>0f>0 everywhere for the interlaced state and its flavor orientation defines a smooth CP2 texture. On the common three-flux magnetic cell it carries Qsk=−3Q_{\rm sk}=-3. For comparison we also use a coincident-core trial state, built from the same three lattices without the displacement (𝐝=0\mathbf{d}=0). All three components then vanish at the same points, so the total density vanishes there as well and ⟨f2⟩=1.15959527\langle f^{2}\rangle=1.15959527. Its flavor orientation is uniform, so it is an ordinary vortex lattice without a skyrmion texture.

To impose the local Gauss law on this trial field, write 𝐚=𝐚¯+δ​𝐚\mathbf{a}=\bar{\mathbf{a}}+\delta\mathbf{a} and choose a periodic transverse correction of zero mean with ∇×δ​𝐚=−B⁡(f−1)\nabla\times\delta\mathbf{a}=-B(f-1). The orbitals obey the LLL condition in 𝐚¯\bar{\mathbf{a}}, so the first term in the completed square reduces to ℏ2​∫ρ​|δ​𝐚|2/(2​M)\hbar^{2}\int\rho|\delta\mathbf{a}|^{2}/(2M). Thus

EtrialN=elb​⟨f2⟩+ℏ22​M​⟨f​|δ​𝐚|2⟩.\frac{E_{\rm trial}}{N}=e_{\rm lb}\langle f^{2}\rangle+\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2M}\langle f|\delta\mathbf{a}|^{2}\rangle.

For the interlaced lattice the Fourier sum gives ⟨f​|δ​𝐚|2⟩/B=0.00000515\langle f|\delta\mathbf{a}|^{2}\rangle/B=0.00000515. At g=0g=0 the resulting energy per particle is 0.3333730.333373 in units of π​ℏ2​n/M\pi\hbar^{2}n/M, within 0.012%0.012\% of the general lower bound 1/31/3. The coincident-core state gives 0.3926350.392635, 18%18\% above the bound.

The filled-LLL interpretation.

To understand the Hall response, first place the anyons in a uniform imposed field. Choose the orientation for which LLL wavefunctions are holomorphic, and let ℓ\ell be the magnetic length. For a fixed flavor orientation, the hard-core anyon wavefunctions take the form

ΨLLL=∏i<j(zi−zj)1/3F(z1,…,zN)e−∑i|zi|2/(4ℓ2).\Psi_{\rm LLL}=\prod_{i<j}(z_{i}-z_{j})^{1/3}\,F(z_{1},\ldots,z_{N})\,\mathrm{e}^{-\sum_{i}|z_{i}|^{2}/(4\ell^{2})}. (S81)

The fractional power supplies the exchange phase ei​π/3\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/3}, while FF is a regular symmetric holomorphic function. The densest state has F=1F=1, with no additional orbital zeros [102, 103]. On the sphere, the statistical factor has degree (N−1)/3(N-1)/3 in each particle coordinate, so the filled state requires NΦ=(N−1)/3N_{\Phi}=(N-1)/3 flux quanta of the single-particle vector potential. Here one flux quantum is 2​π2\pi. Thus νa=N/NΦ→3\nu_{a}=N/N_{\Phi}\to 3 in the thermodynamic limit: the LLL accommodates three anyons per flux quantum because of their statistics. Increasing NΦN_{\Phi} by one accommodates three more anyons, so the Středa relation gives the Hall coefficient Ca=∂N/∂NΦ=3C_{a}=\partial N/\partial N_{\Phi}=3. This is the anyon IQH state, with all anyons fully occupying the lowest LL.

In the skyrmion Hall crystal, the flavor texture supplies the effective field. Projecting motion onto the local spinor 𝐙\mathbf{Z} gives the vector potential −𝓐-\bm{\mathcal{A}}, with −Qsk-Q_{\rm sk} flux quanta. The reference value Qsk=−N/3Q_{\rm sk}=-N/3 therefore gives the same density-to-flux ratio νa=+3\nu_{a}=+3 as the filled anyon LLL. Thus, in this crystal phase, the anyons form a Ca=3C_{a}=3 integer quantum Hall state due to the spontaneously generated skyrmion texture. This crystal is analogous to the electronic anomalous Hall crystals proposed for rhombohedral pentalayer graphene [104, 105, 106]. In a topologically trivial crystal of doped anyons, by contrast, the anyons are localized and add no Hall response. The total Hall conductance then remains that of the undoped FCI.

The physical Hall response.

The physical probe AcA_{c} is normalized to unit electron charge. An anyon of charge −e∗-e_{*}, with e∗=e/3e_{*}=e/3, couples to −Ac/3-A_{c}/3. Its Ca=3C_{a}=3 IQH response therefore contributes 3(−Ac/3)d(−Ac/3)/(4π)=+AcdAc/(12π)3(-A_{c}/3)d(-A_{c}/3)/(4\pi)=+A_{c}\,dA_{c}/(12\pi). The coefficient of Ac​d​Ac/(4​π)A_{c}\,dA_{c}/(4\pi) is 1/31/3, because the fractional charge enters twice. This cancels the parent FCI response −AcdAc/(12π)-A_{c}\,dA_{c}/(12\pi):

σx​y=σFCI+3​e∗2h=−e23​h+e23​h=0.\sigma_{xy}=\sigma_{\rm FCI}+3\frac{e_{*}^{2}}{h}=-\frac{e^{2}}{3h}+\frac{e^{2}}{3h}=0. (S82)

The same conclusion follows directly from the original CB action, Eq. (S78). With the texture pinned, the CB condensate completely Higgses aμa_{\mu}. Integrating out its massive fluctuations leaves no Ac​d​AcA_{c}\,dA_{c} term at long wavelengths. Because ϕ\bm{\phi} has unit gauge charge, no residual discrete gauge group remains. The final phase is therefore a topologically trivial charge insulator, with broken translation and flavor symmetries. For the ν=2/3\nu=2/3 FCI in tMoTe2, the Hall crystal of doped anyons adds e2/(3​h)e^{2}/(3h) to the parent response 2​e2/(3​h)2e^{2}/(3h). The resulting RIQAH insulator has σx​y=e2/h\sigma_{xy}=e^{2}/h.

Relation to the commensurate FCI-CDW transition

The transition studied in Ref. [82] at fixed filling ν=2/3\nu=2/3 has the same three-component condensation mechanism. In our chirality convention, their three dual-vortex fields play the role of ϕ\bm{\phi} in Eq. (S78), with a common gauge field and the same level-three Chern–Simons term. The matter fields are relativistic in that transition theory. When they are gapped, the fractional Hall response combines with the filled C=1C=1 band to give σx​y=2​e2/(3​h)\sigma_{xy}=2e^{2}/(3h). Condensation Higgses aa and gives an IQH phase with σx​y=e2/h\sigma_{xy}=e^{2}/h. Because lattice translations act projectively on the three fields, their condensation also produces a commensurate CDW. Its order parameters are gauge-invariant bilinears of the fields, encoded in the CP2 orientation.

The distinction upon doping is the net anyon density. In the undoped case at fixed ν=2/3\nu=2/3, a relativistic condensate does not require a finite average statistical flux. Doping populates one sign of the anyons with charge magnitude e/3e/3. Keeping this branch gives the nonrelativistic CB theory used above. For anyons of charge −e/3-e/3 at density nn, the equation of motion gives

δ​ρele=ba2​π=−n3,\frac{\delta\rho_{\rm el}}{e}=\frac{b_{a}}{2\pi}=-\frac{n}{3}, (S83)

where δ​ρel\delta\rho_{\rm el} is the charge density relative to the commensurate state, at zero applied magnetic field. The resulting flux requires a vortex density n/3n/3 in each component of the condensate. Near the SU(3) limit, the cores can separate to form the smooth skyrmion texture described above.

The skyrmion Hall crystal is therefore a candidate extension of the commensurate IQH-CDW phase to finite doping. The doped density sets the additional texture scale, ℓv∼(n/3)−1/2\ell_{v}\sim(n/3)^{-1/2}, which can greatly exceed the moiré period.

S5 Numerical results

Table S2 compares the lowest-energy liquid and crystal of each system. The subsections below give the detailed results.

S5.1 Semions

Energies.

Table S3 compares the energies of all trial states at the background charges of Fig. 1, qb​g=−3/2q_{bg}=-3/2 for spinless and qb​g=−1/2q_{bg}=-1/2 for SU(2) semions. In these sectors the CF flux 2​Q∗=qb​g+(N−1)/22Q^{*}=q_{bg}+(N-1)/2 lets the CF ν∗=2\nu^{*}=2 state fill two complete Landau levels, or one per spin, at every even NN, so that its shells are closed and it is rotation invariant. Up to N=24N=24, the CF ν∗=2\nu^{*}=2 state and the CF networks initialized with random orbitals converge to the same uniform liquid, with energies within 0.010.01 of each other. So does the optimized Nc=2N_{c}=2 color superconductor, which we trained only up to N=12N=12 because the color sum with backflow becomes too costly; its parameter-free analytical form needs no training and no backflow, and Table S3 gives it up to N=24N=24. For N≥32N\geq 32 the randomly initialized networks lose rotation invariance, and at N=40N=40 they end in non-uniform states with energy 0.060.06 above the CF ν∗=2\nu^{*}=2 state, which indicates that their optimization is trapped in a local minimum. The parameter-free analytical wavefunctions of Eqs. (S39) and (S40) come close to these optimized states. For SU(2) semions the analytical state lies below all of them, by 0.002–0.011 at N=8N=8–24, and for spinless semions it lies 0.007–0.016 above them. This suggests that the color-superconductor wavefunctions are close to the ground state, particularly for SU(2) semions.

Overlaps.

To test whether the liquids obtained from these different constructions describe the same phase, we compute the fidelity F=|⟨A|B⟩|2/(⟨A|A⟩​⟨B|B⟩)F=|\langle A|B\rangle|^{2}/(\langle A|A\rangle\langle B|B\rangle) between trained states (Table S4). Here AA and BB are the full anyonic amplitudes Ψ\Psi, including the statistical factor of the gauge in which each state is built, so that states built in the CF and CB gauges can be compared. Since ⟨A|B⟩/⟨A|A⟩=⟨B/A⟩|A|2\langle A|B\rangle/\langle A|A\rangle=\langle B/A\rangle_{|A|^{2}} and ⟨B|B⟩/⟨A|A⟩=⟨|B/A|2⟩|A|2\langle B|B\rangle/\langle A|A\rangle=\langle|B/A|^{2}\rangle_{|A|^{2}}, where ⟨⋯⟩|A|2\langle\cdots\rangle_{|A|^{2}} averages over configurations sampled from |A|2|A|^{2}, samples of AA alone give the one-sided estimate F=|⟨B/A⟩|A|2|2/⟨|B/A|2⟩|A|2F=|\langle B/A\rangle_{|A|^{2}}|^{2}/\langle|B/A|^{2}\rangle_{|A|^{2}}. Sampling both states gives the two-sided estimate F=⟨B/A⟩|A|2​⟨A/B⟩|B|2F=\langle B/A\rangle_{|A|^{2}}\langle A/B\rangle_{|B|^{2}}, which we use as a check. The liquids differ in construction: the CF ν∗=2\nu^{*}=2 state of Eq. (S15) fills CF Landau levels, the CF networks start from random orbitals instead of filled levels, and the Nc=2N_{c}=2 color superconductor of Eq. (S21) arises from color-singlet pairing of the holon metal. Nevertheless, they have mutual fidelities of 0.950.95–0.9970.997 at N=8N=8 and 12, whereas their fidelities with the CB crystal are only 0.020.02–0.50.5 and decrease rapidly with NN. The independent liquid constructions therefore describe the same state. In particular, the Nc=2N_{c}=2 color superconductor is in the same phase as Laughlin’s original anyon superfluid, the ν∗=2\nu^{*}=2 IQH state of composite fermions [7].

Disk.

To check the sphere results, we study planar versions of the same states on a disk of radius R=N/π​nR=\sqrt{N/\pi n} with a hard wall (Fig. S6). They use the planar coordinates ziz_{i} and zi​jz_{ij} in place of the spinors and wi​jw_{ij}, together with a hard-wall factor ∏i(1−ri2/R2)\prod_{i}(1-r_{i}^{2}/R^{2}) and a learned one-body Jastrow factor. As on the sphere, the CF ν∗=2\nu^{*}=2 state occupies the two lowest Landau levels of the mean CF field, or one per spin, and the CF networks start from these Landau-level orbitals or from random ones. We call the lowest of these CF states at each NN the CF liquid. The CB vortex lattice is the planar counterpart of the one on the sphere, Φ=∏i<jri​jα​∏i,k(z¯i−v¯k)/R\Phi=\prod_{i<j}r_{ij}^{\alpha}\prod_{i,k}(\bar{z}_{i}-\bar{v}_{k})/R with learned vortex positions vkv_{k}. The CF liquid lies well below the CB vortex lattice at every NN, with energy differences of 0.180.18 for spinless semions and 0.420.42 for SU(2) semions at N=30N=30. Accounting for the edge contribution of order N−1/2N^{-1/2}, we fit the CF liquid energies to E/N=e∞+a/N+b/NE/N=e_{\infty}+a/\sqrt{N}+b/N over N=12N=12–56. The extrapolated values, e∞=0.809​(17)e_{\infty}=0.809(17) for spinless semions and 0.557​(10)0.557(10) for SU(2) semions, agree within two standard errors with the sphere results 0.7837​(4)0.7837(4) and 0.5407​(7)0.5407(7).

Pair correlator.

The pair density matrix ρ2​(R,R′)=⟨Δ†​(R′)​Δ​(R)⟩\rho_{2}(R,R^{\prime})=\langle\Delta^{\dagger}(R^{\prime})\Delta(R)\rangle, with Δ⁡(R)\Delta(R) removing two anyons near RR, is estimated in the trained state by moving a pair rigidly. For a configuration ZZ sampled from |Ψ|2|\Psi|^{2}, we pick an anyon at random and its nearest partner within c2=0.6n−1/2c_{2}=0.6\,n^{-1/2} (for SU(2), of the opposite or of the same spin). We rotate both by an angle γ\gamma about the axis through the center of the sphere perpendicular to the pair’s center. The pair thus moves along a great circle by the arc length R​γR\gamma with its internal configuration unchanged. With ZγZ_{\gamma} the moved configuration,

C2​(γ)=⟨Φ⁡(Zγ)Φ⁡(Z)​ei⁡[S⁡(Zγ)−S⁡(Z)]⟩|Ψ|2,S=∑j∉pair[2​αs​arg⁡wc​j+αs​∑a∈pairarg⁡wa​jwc​j],C_{2}(\gamma)=\Big\langle\frac{\Phi(Z_{\gamma})}{\Phi(Z)}\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}[S(Z_{\gamma})-S(Z)]}\Big\rangle_{|\Psi|^{2}},\qquad S=\sum_{j\notin{\rm pair}}\Big[2\alpha_{s}\arg w_{cj}+\alpha_{s}\sum_{a\in{\rm pair}}\arg\frac{w_{aj}}{w_{cj}}\Big], (S84)

where Φ\Phi is the wavefunction without the statistical factor, in the gauge in which the state is built (αs=α−1\alpha_{s}=\alpha-1 for CF states and αs=α\alpha_{s}=\alpha for CB and color states), and wc​j=uc​vj−vc​ujw_{cj}=u_{c}v_{j}-v_{c}u_{j} is written with the spinor ξc\xi_{c} of the pair’s center. We average over 3×1033\times 10^{3}–2.5×1042.5\times 10^{4} pairs per size and define the plateau as the mean of |C2||C_{2}| over the outer half of the move, γ≥π/2\gamma\geq\pi/2.

The phase SS specifies the anyonic pair operator. Because Ψ\Psi is multivalued, the ratio Ψ⁡(Zγ)/Ψ⁡(Z)\Psi(Z_{\gamma})/\Psi(Z) is fixed only once we specify how the statistical factor between the two moved anyons and the others, ∏a∈pair∏j∉pair(wa​j/|wa​j|)αs\prod_{a\in{\rm pair}}\prod_{j\notin{\rm pair}}(w_{aj}/|w_{aj}|)^{\alpha_{s}}, is continued from ZZ to ZγZ_{\gamma}. This choice is the string carried by Δ\Delta, the analog of a Jordan–Wigner string. For each anyon jj outside the pair we factor

∏a∈pair(wa​j|wa​j|)αs=(wc​j|wc​j|)2​αs​∏a∈pair(wa​j/wc​j|wa​j/wc​j|)αs.\prod_{a\in{\rm pair}}\Big(\frac{w_{aj}}{|w_{aj}|}\Big)^{\alpha_{s}}=\Big(\frac{w_{cj}}{|w_{cj}|}\Big)^{2\alpha_{s}}\prod_{a\in{\rm pair}}\Big(\frac{w_{aj}/w_{cj}}{|w_{aj}/w_{cj}|}\Big)^{\alpha_{s}}.

For semions 2​αs=±12\alpha_{s}=\pm 1, so the first factor is single valued: seen from outside, the pair carries an integer statistical charge and braids trivially with every anyon. The second factor approaches 1 when anyon jj is far from the pair. We take it on the principal branch, xαs=ei​αs​Arg​xx^{\alpha_{s}}=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\alpha_{s}\mathrm{Arg}\,x} with Argx∈(−π,π]\mathrm{Arg}\,x\in(-\pi,\pi] for a unit complex number xx. This phase jumps only where wa​j/wc​jw_{aj}/w_{cj} is negative real, that is, when anyon jj lies on the arc between member aa and the center cc, so the branch cut lies inside the pair. Summed over jj, the phase of the product is SS of Eq. (S84). It is a single-valued function of the configuration that jumps only when another anyon crosses the cut inside the pair, so ei​S\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}S} is the string of the local pair operator Δ=ψ⁡(z1)​ψ​(z2)\Delta=\psi(z_{1})\psi(z_{2}). The local string is essential. The natural alternative is a path string, which continues each factor (wa​j/|wa​j|)αs(w_{aj}/|w_{aj}|)^{\alpha_{s}} continuously along the trajectory of member aa during the rotation, that is, it assigns the statistical phase that the two anyons accumulate when they are transported along their paths. This continued phase agrees with ei​S\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}S} until another anyon passes between the two members, crossing the cut. There the principal-branch factor jumps by e±2​π​i​αs=−1\mathrm{e}^{\pm 2\pi\mathrm{i}\alpha_{s}}=-1, while the continued phase does not, so the two differ by a factor −1-1 for every anyon that passes between the members during the move. These signs depend on the positions of the other anyons and average out, so they would suppress C2C_{2} even in a genuine pair condensate.

Figure S7 shows that |C2||C_{2}| for the CF ν∗=2\nu^{*}=2 state decreases over one to two interparticle spacings and then approaches a plateau, both for spinless semions and for opposite-spin pairs of SU(2) semions. The plateau decreases with NN only approximately as N−0.16N^{-0.16}, much more slowly than the N−1/2N^{-1/2} decay of the bare CF state (Sec. S4.2). The Nc=2N_{c}=2 color superconductor has the same pair correlator, as Fig. S7(c) shows. For the analytical wavefunction this agreement requires the long-range Jastrow factor. Without Ji​jJ_{ij}, the color sum keeps its plasma-like long-distance correlations (Sec. S3), and the opposite-spin plateau falls well below the CF value [Fig. S7(d)].

Structure factor.

The density structure factor S⁡(l)=1N​∑i​jPl​(cos⁡θi​j)S(l)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{ij}P_{l}(\cos\theta_{ij}) at q=l/Rq=l/R is shown in Fig. S8. At N=12N=12 the CF ν∗=2\nu^{*}=2 state, the random-start networks and the Nc=2N_{c}=2 color superconductor have the same S⁡(q)S(q), to within 0.010.01 (spinless) and 0.020.02 [SU(2)], as their overlaps (Table S4) require; at this size the crystal’s S⁡(q)S(q) is still close to theirs. At the smallest wave vector q1=1/Rq_{1}=1/R the CF state has S⁡(q1)/q1​a0=0.29S(q_{1})/q_{1}a_{0}=0.29–0.320.32 (spinless, N=8N=8–40) and 0.340.34–0.360.36 [SU(2), N=8N=8–24], with a0=n−1/2a_{0}=n^{-1/2}, nearly independent of NN, while S⁡(q1)/(q1​a0)2S(q_{1})/(q_{1}a_{0})^{2} grows with NN. Thus S⁡(q)S(q) is linear in qq, rather than quadratic as for an incompressible quantum Hall state such as the bare CF state.

A linear S⁡(q)S(q) alone does not distinguish the superfluid from the crystal. The statistical vector potentials cancel in pairs, ∑i𝐚⁡(𝐫i)=0\sum_{i}\mathbf{a}(\mathbf{r}_{i})=0, so the total momentum is conserved. At long wavelengths the statistical fields b=−2​π​αs​ρb=-2\pi\alpha_{s}\rho and 𝐞=−2παs𝐳^×𝐣\mathbf{e}=-2\pi\alpha_{s}\hat{\mathbf{z}}\times\mathbf{j} exert no net force, ρ​𝐞+𝐣×b​𝐳^=0\rho\,\mathbf{e}+\mathbf{j}\times b\,\hat{\mathbf{z}}=0, so no cyclotron gap appears. The weight of the ff-sum rule at small qq is then carried by a gapless longitudinal mode, the sound of the superfluid or the longitudinal phonon of the crystal. If cc is its velocity, then in both phases

S⁡(q)≃s​q,s=ℏ2​m​c.S(q)\simeq s\,q,\qquad s=\frac{\hbar}{2mc}.

The velocity is set by how strongly the system resists the deformation that a long-wavelength longitudinal wave produces. Resistance to compression is measured by the bulk modulus K=n​∂P/∂nK=n\,\partial P/\partial n, where PP is the pressure: a small density change δ​n\delta n raises the pressure by δ​P=K​δ​n/n\delta P=K\,\delta n/n. Resistance to a change of shape at fixed area is measured by the shear modulus μs\mu_{s}, which vanishes in a liquid and is positive in a crystal. A longitudinal wave 𝐮∝𝐱^​cos⁡q​x\mathbf{u}\propto\hat{\mathbf{x}}\cos qx stretches the medium along 𝐱^\hat{\mathbf{x}} only, which both changes its area and changes its shape, so elasticity theory gives

m​n​c2=K(superfluid),m​n​c2=K+μs(crystal),mn\,c^{2}=K\quad\text{(superfluid)},\qquad mn\,c^{2}=K+\mu_{s}\quad\text{(crystal)},

with m​nmn the mass density. Scale invariance fixes KK in every phase through its own e∞e_{\infty}. At zero temperature P=n2​∂(E/N)/∂nP=n^{2}\,\partial(E/N)/\partial n, and E/N=e∞​π​ℏ2​n/mE/N=e_{\infty}\pi\hbar^{2}n/m gives P=e∞​π​ℏ2​n2/mP=e_{\infty}\pi\hbar^{2}n^{2}/m and K=2​π​e∞​ℏ2​n2/mK=2\pi e_{\infty}\hbar^{2}n^{2}/m. For the shear modulus scale invariance fixes only the form, μs=μ~​π​ℏ2​n2/m\mu_{s}=\tilde{\mu}\,\pi\hbar^{2}n^{2}/m, with a dimensionless coefficient μ~≥0\tilde{\mu}\geq 0 that depends on the crystal. Together,

sa0=12​π⁡(2​e∞+μ~),\frac{s}{a_{0}}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi(2e_{\infty}+\tilde{\mu})}},

where μ~=0\tilde{\mu}=0 gives the superfluid value s=a0/(2​2​π​e∞)s=a_{0}/(2\sqrt{2\pi e_{\infty}}) of Sec. S3. On the sphere the ff-sum rule and the phonon frequency involve l⁡(l+1)/R2l(l+1)/R^{2} instead of q2q^{2}, which raises the ratio at l=1l=1 by 2\sqrt{2}: S⁡(q1)/(q1​a0)=1/{2​[π⁡(e∞+μ~/2)]1/2}S(q_{1})/(q_{1}a_{0})=1/\{2[\pi(e_{\infty}+\tilde{\mu}/2)]^{1/2}\}. For the superfluid this gives 0.320.32 for spinless and 0.380.38 for SU(2) semions, close to the values above. For the crystal, with its higher e∞e_{\infty} of 0.9090.909 and 0.7830.783 (Table S2), it gives 0.300.30 and 0.320.32 at μ~=0\tilde{\mu}=0, and less for μ~>0\tilde{\mu}>0. The CB crystals have S⁡(q1)/(q1​a0)=0.28S(q_{1})/(q_{1}a_{0})=0.28–0.300.30 (spinless) and 0.300.30–0.340.34 [SU(2)] at N=8N=8–24, also nearly independent of NN and comparable to these values. Since the competing states differ in e∞e_{\infty} by less than a factor of 1.5, their slopes ss are similar, and S⁡(q)≃s​qS(q)\simeq s\,q is a common property of the compressible phases.

S5.2 Spinless anyons at θ=π/3\theta=\pi/3

The shift sectors qb​g=−5/3q_{bg}=-5/3, −4/3-4/3, −1-1 and −1/3-1/3 select the Moore–Read, CFL, PH-Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states, respectively, in the second Landau level for the composite fermions, and we initialize the CF liquid in each sector with the corresponding exact wavefunction. Table S5 compares every ansatz with the CB crystal at the same sector and size. For N≥12N\geq 12, the best liquid and crystal differ by less than 0.0150.015 per particle, with the liquid energy relative to the crystal ranging from −0.013-0.013 in the Moore–Read sector at N=14N=14 to +0.008+0.008 in the PH-Pfaffian sector at N=16N=16. The sign changes with both the sector and NN; in the CFL sector, the trion Fermi liquid is lower by 0.0100.010 at N=24N=24. CF networks initialized with random orbitals instead converge to non-uniform states above both candidates. The three-color metal and its 2SC descendants, in which colors 1 and 2 pair while color 3 forms either a closed-shell pocket or pairs with itself, give the lowest energies at N≤9N\leq 9. At N=12N=12, they lie slightly below the crystal in the qb​g=2/3q_{bg}=2/3 and 5/35/3 sectors, where no CF liquid is available, while the CF liquid remains lower in the anti-Pfaffian sector. Taken together, we are not confident to make claims on whether the liquid phase or the crystal phase has lower energy for this case, given how close their energy is. For the liquid phase, the CF and color constructions lead to the same trion liquid. In the CFL sector, the second-level CFs become charge-3 fermions that couple to no gauge field, the trion Fermi liquid of Sec. S4.3. In the color construction, the three-color metal is a fractionalized metal of three holon Fermi seas coupled to the SU(3) gauge field. Pairing colors 1 and 2 breaks the color gauge group, and the remaining pocket of color 3 carries the anyon number 3 of a trion and is neutral under the residual gauge group. The 2SC with an unpaired third color is therefore also a Fermi liquid of trions, with the same Fermi volume n/3n/3. Pairing the trions gives a superfluid of six-anyon clusters, as the Moore–Read, PH-Pfaffian or anti-Pfaffian state of the CFs in the second-Landau-level. Each shift sector admits only one of these CF states, so paired and unpaired trion liquids can be compared only across sectors, where the shift changes the finite-size energy. We therefore cannot determine whether the trion Fermi liquid is unstable to pairing.

S5.3 SU(3) anyons at θ=π/3\theta=\pi/3

Energetics.

The color superconductor has the lowest variational energy among the states considered (Table S6). We compare each liquid with the crystal at the same qb​gq_{bg} and NN, since the shift changes the finite-size correction [Fig. S9(a)]. In both chiral sectors, qb​g=−1/3q_{bg}=-1/3 and 5/35/3, the color superconductor lies below the crystal by an amount that grows with NN, and its extrapolated energy lies well below that of the crystal (Table S2). Because of the shift, the p+i​pp+ip state at qb​g=5/3q_{bg}=5/3 lies below the p−i​pp-ip state at qb​g=−1/3q_{bg}=-1/3 at fixed NN, but it extrapolates above it. Remarkably, the lowest energy requires no optimization: the analytical wavefunction of Eq. (S41), which has no variational parameters, lies slightly below the optimized color superconductor at every size.

Flavor symmetry of the analytical state.

As discussed in Sec. S3.2, the same-color contact factor weakly breaks the flavor symmetry of Eq. (S41). The Casimir test of Sec. S3.2 shows that the state is an exact singlet at N=6N=6 and contains a non-singlet admixture of about 0.15% at N=12N=12, in the 27-dimensional representation. The exact flavor singlet of Eq. (S45) has the same energy at N=6N=6 and a slightly higher one at N=12N=12 and 18, by at most 0.006 per particle.

Comparison with the optimized state.

The analytical wavefunction has a high fidelity with the optimized color superconductor, and the two extrapolate to the same e∞e_{\infty}. The fidelities in Table S7 show that the different constructions of the color superconductor describe the same phase. The color state with only a two-body Jastrow factor and the analytical wavefunction, with the contact correction in all factors or in the pair function only, have −lnF/N-\ln F/N more than an order of magnitude smaller than the competing phases at N≥12N\geq 12. The exception is the SU(3) holon metal at N=18N=18, where two holons per species fill the lowest shell, so that lowest-shell pairing reproduces the closed-shell metal.

S5.4 Skyrmion Hall crystal

Figure S10 shows the crystal at N=36N=36. We locate its vortices by moving one particle of a given flavor over a grid while holding the remaining particles at a configuration sampled from |Ψ|2|\Psi|^{2}. The vortices are not fixed network parameters, since the backflow and environment-dependent coefficients in Eq. (S20) allow them to move with the other particles. Across 48 sampled configurations, the vortices of each flavor cluster around NvN_{v} lattice sites, with rms displacements of 0.2–0.4a0a_{0} compared with site spacings of 1.2–1.5a0a_{0} for N=12N=12–36. This separation of scales defines a well-formed vortex lattice whose vortices fluctuate around their sites, much as particles do in a quantum crystal. The three sublattices interleave, allowing the other two flavors to fill each vortex core, as in interlaced vortex lattices of two-component condensates [98]. Each flavor density vanishes at its own sites and reaches about twice its mean between them, while the total density varies by only about ±10%\pm 10\%, so the dominant modulation is in the flavor texture.

Extracting the texture from the wavefunction.

To extract the flavor texture of the correlated variational state, we sample a configuration from |Ψ|2|\Psi|^{2} and move one flavor-1 anyon to a probe position 𝐫\mathbf{r}, obtaining a CB amplitude z1​(𝐫)z_{1}(\mathbf{r}). We obtain z2z_{2} and z3z_{3} by exchanging the probe’s flavor with that of a fixed reference anyon of the corresponding flavor. The three amplitudes have identical particle positions and total flavor populations. Common factors, including the statistical phase and flavor-independent Jastrow factors, therefore cancel in the ratios z1:z2:z3z_{1}:z_{2}:z_{3}. We thus regard (z1,z2,z3)(z_{1},z_{2},z_{3}) only up to an overall complex factor. This defines a point [z1:z2:z3][z_{1}:z_{2}:z_{3}] of the complex projective plane CP2 in homogeneous coordinates, and 𝐫↦[z1:z2:z3]\mathbf{r}\mapsto[z_{1}:z_{2}:z_{3}] maps the sphere to CP2. Because the reference anyons carry different flavors in the three amplitudes, z2z_{2} and z3z_{3} acquire scale factors relative to z1z_{1}, which bias the flavor weights. We remove this bias by using Zb=wb​zb/(∑cwc​|zc|2)1/2Z_{b}=\sqrt{w_{b}}z_{b}/(\sum_{c}w_{c}|z_{c}|^{2})^{1/2}, with positive constants wbw_{b} chosen so that the spatial average of each |Zb|2|Z_{b}|^{2} is 1/31/3. The wbw_{b} do not depend on 𝐫\mathbf{r}, but we determine them separately for each sampled configuration, since the scale factors depend on the positions of the reference anyons. These nonsingular rescalings preserve the topological charge. For the correlated state, this defines a conditional texture for each sampled configuration. Its averaged flavor weights are compared with the measured densities below.

Numerically, the Berry flux through each grid plaquette is the phase of the cyclic overlap product (𝐙1†​𝐙2)​(𝐙2†​𝐙3)​(𝐙3†​𝐙4)​(𝐙4†​𝐙1)(\mathbf{Z}_{1}^{\dagger}\mathbf{Z}_{2})(\mathbf{Z}_{2}^{\dagger}\mathbf{Z}_{3})(\mathbf{Z}_{3}^{\dagger}\mathbf{Z}_{4})(\mathbf{Z}_{4}^{\dagger}\mathbf{Z}_{1}), where the subscripts label its corners in order. Local phase choices cancel in this product. Summing the plaquette phases and dividing by 2​π2\pi gives QskQ_{\rm sk}; we report its magnitude when comparing it with NvN_{v}. The CP2 map gives |Qsk|=Nv|Q_{\rm sk}|=N_{v} in 46 of the 48 configurations and Nv−1N_{v}-1 in the remaining two, with an average skyrmion charge of 1/31/3 per vortex cell. Averaged over the configurations, the composition |Zb|2|Z_{b}|^{2} of the texture reproduces the flavor fraction ρb/ρ\rho_{b}/\rho measured from the samples, the density of flavor bb divided by the total density: their Pearson correlation coefficient over the sphere is 0.99 for each flavor. The averaged skyrmion density peaks where the total density is lowest. Removing the texture makes the crystal flavor symmetric and raises its energy to that of spinless anyons, by 0.11–0.13 per particle at N=12N=12–24 [Fig. S10(d)]. This SU(3) flavor texture is analogous to the spin textures of quantum Hall skyrmion crystals [107, 108] and spinor Bose condensates [96, 97, 98]. In the doped FCI of twisted MoTe2, the SU(3) flavor is a valley index arising from the projective action of translations on the charge-e/3e/3 anyons, which produces a threefold-degenerate band with three valleys [23, 26, 40]. The flavor texture therefore breaks moiré translation symmetry, and local probes should detect the skyrmion Hall crystal as charge order on the moiré scale.
